Insatiable avarice and swollen arrogance have so blinded him, and indeed driven him mad, that as a trophy and an eternal monument of the deeds we have mentioned, so splendidly performed by himself, he set up for himself a bronze statue at Antwerp (which he himself also built), cast from captured bronze, as his inscription boasts, trampling underfoot the nobility and the Orders of the provinces. Passing over here what he meant by erecting that statue, when have we ever read in any history of a tyrant who, while still alive, set up a statue to himself? Certainly the Roman Caesars and kings, who had subdued almost the whole world, sometimes allowed statues of stone or bronze to be erected to them, as the Roman Pontiffs, who boast of being God's vicars, do today. Yet this was always done by the command and authority of the Senate or the people, or at least with their consent and with goodwill intervening. But that tyrants, while still alive, decreed such a thing for themselves can be shown by no examples. For what could be more evident proof of some mad insanity and intolerable pride?

units.la: Cæterum hic tyrannus, vt reliquos tyrannos omnes tam vesana quadam atrogantia, quam horrenda crudelitate superaret, perinde ac si non Regiam tantum, verum etiam diuinam Maiestatem affectaret, sibi ipse viuus statuam hanc ludibrii plenam, nullo cuiusq; consilio, approbatione, vel auctoritate intercedente, in magnam Regiæ Maiestatis tuæ dignitatis, auctoritatisque imminutionem & despectum, & in quandam tyrannidis effrenataque violentiæ suæ, qua hasce Prouincias tuas quodammodo protriuit, ostentationem ac trophæum erigi curauit.
units.tr: Moreover, this tyrant, to outdo all other tyrants in a certain mad arrogance and horrible cruelty, as if he aspired not only to royal but to divine majesty, had a statue of himself erected while still alive. It is full of mockery. He had it put up without anyone's counsel, approval or authority, to the great diminution and disgrace of the dignity and authority of Your Royal Majesty, and as a display and trophy of his unbridled tyranny and violence, by which he has in a manner trampled these your Provinces.

units.la: Pari etiam vesania veritus non est, ad exemplum Herodis illius tyranni, Antuerpiæ in medio foro Regiæ Maiestatis tuæ solium omnibus ante hac Principum vicariis intactum conscendere, ostroque, quo totum illud obductum erat, insidere: ac ve-
units.tr: With similar madness, and after the example of that tyrant Herod, he was not afraid to mount, in the middle of the forum at Antwerp, the throne of Your Royal Majesty, which no vicar of the princes before him had ever touched, and to sit upon it, covered with the purple with which the whole thing was draped; and ac ve-

units.la: M ac veluti Regiæ Maiestatis tuæ Simulachrum atque idolum, prætextu promulgandæ Absolutionis, sese spectandum præbere: quod à nemine vnquam, ne Regina quidem, aut alio quouis Principe, qui hasce Prouincias gubernarunt, tentatum fuit. Quæ omnia quis non videt ad manifestum contemptum magnamque Regiæ dignitatis tuæ existimationisque imminutionem pertinere.
units.tr: And as if to present himself as the image and idol of Your Royal Majesty, under the pretext of proclaiming the Absolution, he displayed himself to be gazed upon. No one has ever attempted this, not the Queen nor any other prince who governed these Provinces. Who does not see that all these things pertain to manifest contempt and a great diminution of the dignity and reputation of Your Royal Majesty?

units.la: Hæc omnia, clementissime Rex, ita iam omnibus nota, ac per vniuersum terrarum orbem peruulgata sunt, vt omnes exteræ nationes, & Principes adeo impotentem arrogantiam, immanemque crudelitatem perhorrescere coeperint: adeo vt & ipsi Ducis Albani administri ac milites satis profitentur, se eiuscemodi res nulla ratione vt bonas æquasque probare posse: tantum abest, vt ad Maiestatis tuæ ac Prouinciæ commodum dignitatemque spectare arbitrentur.
units.tr: All these things, most merciful King, are now so well known to everyone and so widely published throughout the whole world that all foreign nations and princes have begun to abhor such unbridled arrogance and monstrous cruelty. So much so, that even the servants and soldiers of the Duke of Alba openly declare that they cannot in any way approve such things as good and just. They are so far from thinking that these things tend to the advantage and dignity of Your Majesty and the Province.

units.la: Quamobrem nullo pacto nobis persuadere possumus, Maiestatem tuam adeo horrendæ oppressioni, immanique violentiæ atque impotenti vesaniæ locum daturam, si rei ipsius veritas paulo penitius tibi declarata esset. Quis enim vnquam Rex aut Princeps adeo inhumaniter se erga suos subditos gessit? Maiores tui, clementissime Rex, tantam benignitatem, & clementiam moderationemque Principibus dignam, erga subditos suos præ se tulerunt, vt non solum successoribus suis, verum etiam omnibus Christiani ordinis Principibus præclarum virtutum suarum exemplum ad imitandum reliquerint. Quinimo si quando subditi, præfectorum Regiorum culpa, aut alia huius generis de causa arma sumpsissent, iterumque ad Principis suæ obedientiam reducti essent: nunquam tamen res eo processit, vt eius modi exempla crudelitatis vnquam edere vellent. Quinpotius, quoties de componenda discordia ageretur, summa cura diligentiaque cauerunt, vt ad singula tractationis capita speciatim declararetur, Principes omnia ipsorum priuilegia
units.tr: Therefore we cannot in any way persuade ourselves that Your Majesty would permit such dreadful oppression, monstrous violence and frenzied madness, if the truth of the matter were made known to you more thoroughly. For what king or prince has ever behaved so inhumanely towards his subjects? Your ancestors, most merciful King, showed such kindness, clemency and moderation, worthy of princes, towards their subjects that they have left to their successors, and to all princes of the Christian order, a splendid example of their virtues to imitate. Indeed, if at any time subjects had taken up arms through the fault of royal officials or for some other reason of this kind, and had then been brought back to obedience to their prince, matters never went so far that they wished to display such examples of cruelty. Rather, whenever there was question of composing a dispute, they took the greatest care and diligence that each point of the negotiation should be declared specifically, namely that the princes would preserve all the privileges of their subjects,

units.la: Etiamsi subditi rebellassent, tamen tanta crudelitas non est adhibita. priuilegia, immunitates ac iura integra conseruaturos sanctequE, & inuiolabiliter obseruaturos.
units.tr: Even if the subjects had rebelled, still such cruelty was not employed. privileges, immunities and rights entire, and would keep them sacredly and inviolably.

units.la: Adeo vt insignem Regiæ Maiestati tuæ iniuriam facturos esse sibi persuadeant, si eo se adduci sinant, vt credant Maiestatem tuam à præclaro maiorum suorum exemplo, imo ab officio boni Regis ac Principis descisse. Quod quidem faceret, si subtracta fidelibus subditis suis iustitiæ administratione, & negata miserabilibus ipsorum querelis audientia, tyrannum ipsis aliquem mitteret, qui omnes ex æquo crudeliter trucidaret, deuastaret, & in perpetuam durissimamque seruitutem pertraheret.
units.tr: So that they are persuaded that Your Royal Majesty would do a notable wrong to them if they allowed themselves to believe that Your Majesty had departed from the splendid example of your ancestors, indeed from the duty of a good king and prince. This would indeed be the case if, with the administration of justice withdrawn from your loyal subjects and a hearing denied to their wretched complaints, you were to send them some tyrant who would cruelly slaughter and lay waste all alike, and drag them into perpetual and most harsh slavery.

units.la: Quocirca cum nunc Dux Albanus adeo frequenter nobis suam absolutionem proponat, perinde ac si Maiestatis tuæ nomine anteacta crimina commissa rebellionemque (vt ipse vocat) nobis condonare velit, nulla ratione eam admittere possumus, absq; summa Regiæ Maiestatis tuæ dignitatisq; iactura. Hoc enim nobis certissimo persuademus, Maiestate tuâ nulla ratione nos aperti criminis rebellionisq; damnaturam, quin prius nos audierit, causæq; nostræ æquitate cognoverit.
units.tr: Wherefore, since the Duke of Alba now so often offers us his absolution, as if he were willing, in Your Majesty's name, to pardon us for past crimes and for rebellion (as he calls it), we cannot in any way accept it without the greatest loss to the dignity of Your Royal Majesty. For we are most firmly persuaded that Your Majesty will in no way condemn us of open crime and rebellion before you have heard us and examined the justice of our cause.

units.la: Nunc vero quis est, qui horum aliquid Maiestati tuæ vnquam declarauerit? Aut quis vnquam à Maiestate tua auditus fuit, nisi apertus hostis, & capitalis inimicus? Quum tamen hoc satis omnibus constet, vtramque partem audiendam esse, priusquam sententia ferri queat? Quo quidem nomine veteres historiæ Alexandrum Magnum vehementer commendant: qui quotiescunq; alteram partem audiret, capite in cubitum inclinato, alteram auriculam obstructam seruabat: rogatusq; quo consilio id faceret, respondebat: Vt alteri etiam parti plenam integramq; auriculâ præbere posset, æque ac priori. Quod certe apud omnes gentes atq; nationes magnam æquitatis moderationisq; laude inuenit, & iuri naturali plane consentaneum est; adeo vt nemo maleficus, quantumuis atrocia facinora commiserit, damnari vnquam possit, nisi purgatione defensioneq; eius antea audita.
units.tr: But who has ever declared any of these things to Your Majesty? Or who has ever been heard by Your Majesty, except an open enemy and mortal foe? Yet it is agreed by all that both parties should be heard before sentence can be passed. On this point the ancient histories greatly commend Alexander the Great, who, whenever he heard one party, kept his head bowed onto his elbow and one ear stopped up. When asked why he did this, he answered: so that I may give the other party also a full and unimpaired ear, just as to the first. This certainly wins great praise for fairness and moderation among all peoples and nations, and is entirely consistent with natural law. So no wrongdoer, however atrocious the crimes he has committed, can ever be condemned unless his defence and purgation have first been heard.

units.la: Nunc igitur, clementissime Rex, ad Maiestatis tuæ pedes prostrati supplicitèr oramus, vt nobis alteram aurem accommodare, causamque nostram æquitatis trutina examinare velis. Maiestas tua nihil hactenus præter Ducis Albani, eiusque Assectarum nuntios, epistolas, instructionesq; accepit, & abillis solis rerum statum cognouit. Fauces nobis hactenus obturatæ fuerunt, linguæ ignitis ferris transfixæ, labia candentibus forcipibus constricta, ne de ærumnis nostris miseriisque conqueri possemus, viæ etiam obsessæ obstructæq; fuerunt, ita vt neque literæ nostræ, neque ploratus ad Maiestatem tuam perrumpere potuerint.
units.tr: Now therefore, most merciful King, we prostrate ourselves at Your Majesty's feet and humbly pray that you would be pleased to lend us your other ear and weigh our cause in the balance of justice. Until now Your Majesty has received nothing but the messages, letters and instructions of the Duke of Alba and his followers, and has learned the state of affairs from them alone. Our throats have hitherto been stopped up, our tongues pierced with red-hot irons, our lips clamped with glowing pincers, so that we could not complain of our troubles and miseries. The roads too have been beset and blocked, so that neither our letters nor our lamentations could break through to Your Majesty.

units.la: Quonam igitur pacto Maiestas tua nos alicuius criminis, nedum rebellionis, seditionisque (quam per omnem vitam nostram execrati sumus) merito damnare posset? Idcirco cum nunc Dux Albanus absolutionis suæ diplomata nobis proponit, eaque ratione nos ad suum imperium reducere conatur, cum videat, se nulla vi (admirabili Dei benignitate ac misericordia) ad vesaniæ suæ metam peruenire posse, quo pacto illa acceptabimus, tanquam ad nos pertinentia, qui nunquam nos à debita Maiestati tuæ obedientia abduci vel auelli passi sumus? nisi forte Albanum in locum nostri Regis suscipere agnoscereque velimus. Illi enim soli restitimus, non tuæ Maiestati, cui sanguinem & fortunas nostras ad extremum vitæ spiritum libenter impendere cupimus. Ideoque illius absolutionem nihil ad nos pertinere iudicamus, quæ cum iis tantum Ciuitatibus agit, quæ se à Regis obedientia abduci passæ sunt.
units.tr: By what means, then, could Your Majesty rightly condemn us of any crime, let alone of rebellion and sedition, which we have detested throughout our whole lives? Therefore, since the Duke of Alba now offers us the documents of his absolution, and by this means tries to bring us back under his rule, seeing that he cannot by any force (by the wonderful goodness and mercy of God) reach the goal of his madness, how could we accept them as pertaining to us, who have never allowed ourselves to be drawn away or torn from due obedience to Your Majesty? Unless, perhaps, we were willing to receive Alba and acknowledge him in place of our King. For it is against him alone that we have resisted, not against Your Majesty, to whom we desire to give our blood and fortunes gladly, to our last breath. Therefore we judge his absolution to have nothing to do with us, since it deals only with those cities which have allowed themselves to be drawn away from the obedience of the King.

units.la: Cæterum facile intelligimus, quid hoc facto in animo habeat, nimirum vt se nostrum statuat, aut saltem vt nos fraudulenta eius absolutione pellecti, nostri ipsorum iudices simus, sententiamque de nobis ipsi feramus. Si enim eius absolutionem suscipimus, profecto rebellionis, excitaræq; aduersus Regem nostrum seditionis culpam agnoscimus, imo etiam hæreseos defectionisque à Christiana fide, atque, vt summatim dicam, læsæ atq; imminutæ diuinæ simul & Regiæ Maiestat. reos nos statuimus. tuimus. Hoc ipsum enititur, vt nos acceptione fictitiæ falsæque absolutionis, veluti nostro chirographo subscribamus & consignemus, vt hoc pacto in posterum se apud Maiestatem tuam aliosque Principes excusare purgareque possit, & horrendam suam tyrannidem velare; dicens: nisi eiusce modi flagitia, quæ adeo atroces poenas, grauiaque supplicia merentur, commisissemus, nos veniam absolutionemque nulla ratione admissuros fuisse.
units.tr: Moreover, we easily understand what he has in mind by this act: namely, to make us his own, or at least, by enticing us with his fraudulent absolution, to make ourselves our own judges and pass sentence on ourselves. For if we accept his absolution, we would certainly acknowledge the guilt of rebellion and sedition against our King, indeed also of heresy and defection from the Christian faith, and, to put it briefly, we would declare ourselves guilty of injuring and diminishing both the divine and the royal majesty. This is exactly what he strives for: that by accepting a feigned and false absolution we should subscribe and seal it with our own hand, so that in this way he might afterwards excuse and clear himself before Your Majesty and the other princes, and cloak his dreadful tyranny, saying: unless we had committed such crimes as deserve such atrocious penalties and grave punishments, we would never have admitted pardon and absolution.

units.la: Hic vero Deum Opt. Max. (cui omnes arcani cordium recessus sunt explorati) & Maiestatem tuam obtestamur, nos, si quod eiusmodi scelerum machinati sumus, qualium nos illa absolutio insimulat, veniam nullam precari, imo potius libenter, veluti teterrimæ humani generis pestes, flagitiorum poenas capitibus nostris luere volumus, neque vlla ratione recusamus, clementissime Rex, vt in omnes nos ex æquo exquisitis suppliciis animadvertatur, vtq; membratim discerpamur, modo eiusce modi atrocium flagitiorum rei esse conuincamur. Quinimo rogam⁹ Ducem Albanum (si vllæ modo preces apud eum locum inuenire possunt) vt quotquot ad illum confugerint, impetrandæ illius veniæ absolutionisq; causa, modo seiis, de quibus accusantur, sceleribus obnoxios esse profiteantur, culpamque agnoscant, in eos, nulla adhibita misericordia, prout eiusce modi criminum ratio postulat, animadvertat.
units.tr: Here we call to witness God, Most Good and Most Great, to whom all the secret recesses of hearts are known, and Your Majesty, that if we had devised any crime of the kind with which that absolution charges us, we would not seek any pardon. Rather, like the most foul pests of mankind, we would gladly pay the penalty for our crimes with our heads. Nor do we refuse, most merciful King, that we be punished alike, with exquisite tortures, and torn limb from limb, provided we are proved guilty of crimes of such an atrocious kind. Indeed, we ask the Duke of Alba (if any prayers can find a place with him) that whoever have fled to him in order to obtain that pardon and absolution, provided they profess that they are liable to the crimes of which they are accused and acknowledge their guilt, he punish without any mercy, as the nature of such crimes demands.

units.la: Cæterum, nullus vnquam comperiet, nos illiusce modi aliquid vel leui cogitatione concepisse, tantum abest, vt re ipsa commiserimus. Siquidem Regi summam perpetuo obedientiam, obseruantiamque detulimus. Deum etiam omnipotentem, & Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi in Spiritu & veritate iuxta sanctum præceptum ac verbum ipsius semper, quatenus per virium nostrarum imbecillitatem licuit, colere studuimus, idemque ad extremum vsque vitæ Spiritum præstare parati sumus. At vero cum sensimus, Ducem Albanum loco administrandæ iustitiæ, & querimonias nostras exaudiendi, & promissa, pactaq; tua exequendi, nos præter omne ius & æquū, contracontraque omnia nostra priuilegia atq; immunitates inaudita horrendaque tyrannide opprimere, totamque Prouinciam euertere, multoque crudelius in nos, quam vnquam aut Turcæ aut Saraceni in hostes suos debellatos sæuire, atq; interea nos apud Maiestatem tuam, & apud Christianos Principes falsis criminationibus defectionis, rebellionis, & hæreseos onerare, ita vt omnis audientia nobis negaretur, neque alicunde nobis vlla solatii spes affulgeret, violenta quadam necessitate ad arma capiendum impulsi sumus, & ad omnia remedia tentandum, quibus miserè oppressam patriam nostram ab huiusmodi horrenda tyrannide vindicare possemus, potiusque ad vnum omnes interire, quam vt nos in eiuscemodi tyranni potestatem dedamus. In qua quidem sententia firmiter adhuc persistemus, nisi Maiestas tua benignitatis suæ oculos ad nos deflectere, nostrisque querelis accommodare dignetur, vt nos ex iure & æquo aduersus tantam violentiam tueatur. Neque enim adeo male in sacris literis instituti sumus, quin sciamus, vitam & mortem nostram in DEI manu sitam esse, & mortem hanc nostram, quam nemo mortalium subterfugere potest, nihil aliud esse, quam transitum commigrationemque in vitam illam sempiternam.
units.tr: Moreover, no one will ever find that we have conceived anything of this kind, even in a slight thought, let alone actually committed it. We have shown the King the highest and constant obedience and reverence. We have also striven always, as far as the weakness of our powers allowed, to worship almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, in spirit and truth, according to his holy precept and word, and we are ready to do the same to the last breath of life. But when we perceived that the Duke of Alba, instead of administering justice, hearing our complaints and carrying out your promises and pacts, was oppressing us beyond all law and right and against all our privileges and immunities, with unheard-of and horrible tyranny, and was overthrowing the whole province, raging against us far more cruelly than the Turks or Saracens ever raged against their defeated enemies, while meanwhile burdening us before your Majesty and the Christian princes with false charges of defection, rebellion and heresy, so that every hearing was denied us and no hope of comfort shone on us from anywhere, we were driven by a violent necessity to take up arms and to attempt every remedy by which we could rescue our wretchedly oppressed country from such horrible tyranny, and would rather all perish together than surrender ourselves to the power of such a tyrant. In this resolve we still firmly persist, unless your Majesty deigns to turn the eyes of your kindness toward us and to attend to our complaints, so as to protect us by right and justice against such great violence. For we are not so badly instructed in the sacred letters that we do not know that our life and death lie in the hand of God, and that this death of ours, which no mortal can escape, is nothing other than a passage and migration into that eternal life.

units.la: Quocirca cum mors nostra aliis oblectamento sit, honestă mortem pro libertate ac salute patriæ nostræ oppetere malumus, q; in eiusmodi seruitutem venire, vt proteruam exterorū hominum insolentiam alere debeamus, qui perpetuo in nos ingenti quodā odio atq; inuidia flagrarunt. Certe posteris nostris eam famam ac gloriam relinquemus, vt honeste gloriari possint, iis se maioribus ortos, qui Hispanicorū Inquisitorum serui esse noluerint, quiq; veriti non fuerint, vitam ignominiosam honesta morte redimere. Pugnamus pro libertate nostrarum conscientiarum, vxorum, liberorum, atq; adeo bonorum capitumq; nostrorum: Nimirum, an Dux Alb. cum sua factione violentum in ea imperiū sit habiturus, vt de iis pro suo arbitratu libidineq; decernat? an v. nos ea armata manu pro Dei cultu & clementissimæ Maiestatis tuæ dignitate ad extremum vsq; vitæ spiritum protegemus atq; tuebimur. Scimus, vitæ nostræ certos præfixos limites, quos Albanicæ absolutionis auxilio nequicquam excedemus. Idcirco hoc unum petimus, & obnixe oramus, vt M. T. querimonias nostras audire, remq; ipsam cognoscere dignetur, ne cogamur eiusce modi absolutionis admissione nobis, posterisq; nostris adeo fœdam ac turpem ignominiæ notam, nimirum rebellionis aduersus Deum & Regem, (qua quidem nunquam laborauimus) inurere.
units.tr: Wherefore, since our death is a comfort to others, we prefer to meet an honourable death for the liberty and safety of our country rather than come into such servitude that we must nourish the insolence of foreigners, who have continually blazed against us with a certain great hatred and envy. Certainly we shall leave our posterity the reputation and glory that they may honourably boast of being born of those ancestors who would not be slaves of the Spanish Inquisitors, and who did not fear to redeem an ignominious life with an honourable death. We fight for the liberty of our consciences, our wives, our children, and indeed our goods and our heads. Namely: will the Duke of Alba, with his faction, have violent power over these, to decide about them at his own pleasure and lust? Or shall we protect and defend them with an armed hand, for the worship of God and the dignity of your most clement Majesty, to our last breath? We know the fixed limits set for our life, which we shall vainly exceed by the help of Alban absolution. Therefore we ask only this, and earnestly pray, that Your Majesty deign to hear our complaints and to examine the matter itself, lest we be compelled, by admitting such an absolution, to brand ourselves and our posterity with so foul and shameful a mark of ignominy, namely of rebellion against God and King, which we have never been guilty of.

units.la: Quamuis hoc etiam pro certissimo habemus, etiamsi nobis animus esset suscipiendæ huius absolutionis, eã tamen ob causam Ducem Alb. ceruicibus nostris nequaq; parciturum, imo meliori iure extremam in nobis castigandis seueritatem adhibiturum, q; quidem nunc se consecutû putat, multo etiam honestius se apud quoduis hominû genus excusare posset: Nã ea ipsa ratione, qua nos rebellionis in DEVM & Regê reos agnosceremus, nemo merito forte nostra deploraret, si tanq; hostes atq; perturbatores publicæ tranquillitatis e medio tolleremur.
units.tr: Although we also hold this for quite certain: even if we had the intention of accepting this absolution, the Duke of Alba would not on that account spare our necks. He would rather, with better right, apply the utmost severity in punishing us, which he now thinks he has secured. He could excuse himself far more honourably before any kind of men. For by the very reasoning by which we would acknowledge ourselves guilty of rebellion against God and King, perhaps no one would rightly lament our fate if we were removed from the midst as enemies and disturbers of public tranquillity.

units.la: Atqui etiamsi res ita se non haberet, satis tamen ex omnib. Ducis Alb. actionib. & consiliis liquet, ipsum nihil minus cum animo suo statuisse, q; fidê nobis seruare. Nam præter iusiurandum, q; Ducissa Parmensis, cæteriq; proceres ac gubernatores harû Prouinciarû M.T. nomine Ciuitatib. adeo solemniter pstiterant, violatum in omnib. vrbibus, quas vltimo hoc bello recepit, perfidiâ suam satis declarauit. Montib. Hanoniæ pter iusiurandû & pactû suum qplurimos Ciues in crucem adegit, Nardæ et violatis pactis & promissis suis tam horrendâ cædem excitauit, quanta in tam exigua vrbe nulla vnq; audita fuit. Nũc v. Harlemii, quû ipse, aut saltem Freder. eius filius, ipsius nomine, militû vitæ se parciturû promisisset, eãq; ad rē ꝑceres quid é fidem suã interposuissent, ad vnû omnes, et ad pedisequos vsq; perq; nobiles adolescentes miserabiliter trucidari iussit, eorûq; cadauera nuda, omnibusq; vestimētis exuta, cû summa mulierum virginumq; prꝑtereuntium offensione in publico theatro per integrum diem & noctem exposita esse voluit; Imo eos ipsos, qui vrbem dediderant, & quorum nomina acceperat, suosque stipendiarios fecerat, ad triremes, quæ in quodã Harlemensis portus sinu (Fauces appellant,) substiterant, ablegauit.
units.tr: But even if the matter were not so, it is clear enough from all the Duke of Alba's actions and counsels that he had nothing less in mind than keeping faith with us. For, apart from the oath which the Duchess of Parma and the other nobles and governors of these provinces had solemnly given to the cities in your Majesty's name, he has amply declared his perfidy by violating it in all the towns he took in this last war. At Mons in Hainault, contrary to his oath and his pact, he drove very many citizens to the cross. At Naarden, with his pacts and promises violated, he caused such a slaughter as was never heard of in so small a town. Now at Haarlem, when he himself, or at least his son Frederick in his name, had promised that the soldiers would spare their lives, and the nobles had pledged their faith for this, he ordered all of them, down to the servants and even the noble youths, to be miserably butchered. He wished their naked bodies, stripped of all clothing, to be exposed for a whole day and night in the public theatre, to the great offence of passing women and virgins. Moreover, those very men who had surrendered the town, whose names he had received and whom he had made his paid soldiers, he sent away to the galleys which lay in a bay of the Haarlem harbour (they call it the Fauces).

units.la: Quumque militibus vitam pollicitus esset, fame atque inedia extingui passus est, dicens, se quidem vitam iis pollicitum, victum nequicquam. Quinetiam ciues ipsos Harlemêses, quorum vitæ se parciturum promiserat, vt in obsidione vrbis Alkmarien sis pro fossoribus mererent coegit, vt ibi abeius oppidi incolis miserè trucitarentur. Quod quidem quauis barbarica tyrannide crudelitateque est immanius, merusque prætextus est, quo perfidiæ suæ velum aliquod, & fucum obducere conatur.
units.tr: And when he had promised life to the soldiers, he allowed them to be destroyed by hunger and starvation, saying that he had promised them life, but not food. Moreover, the citizens of Haarlem themselves, whose lives he had promised to spare, he forced to earn their keep as diggers at the siege of the town of Alkmaar, so that there they were miserably butchered by the inhabitants of that town. This is indeed more monstrous than any barbarian tyranny and cruelty, and it is a mere pretext with which he tries to cast some veil and disguise over his perfidy.

units.la: Adeo vt manifestum notissimumque sit, ipsi neque promissa, neque pacta iureiurando confirmata seruandi ac præstandi animum esse, nisi forte ad exiguum aliquod tempus, vt ea ratione facilius ab aliis id quod vult impetret, vtque factum suum aliquando tam apud Maiestatem tuam, quam apud alios Principes probare ac tueri possit. Idcirco nobis hanc absolutionis formulam proponit, quam si ampleƈtemur, fatebimur atque agnoscemus, nos iis criminibus, quorum nos insimulat, fuisse noxios; eaque ipsa ratione neque promissis neque iureiurando præstando ille obstringetur, præcipue cum Concilio Constantiensi ante centum annos sancitum sit, hæreticis fidem seruandam non esse.
units.tr: So it is manifest and most well known that he has no intention of keeping or performing promises and pacts confirmed by oath, except perhaps for a short time, so that by this means he may more easily obtain from others what he wants, and may at some point be able to justify and defend his deed before your Majesty as well as before other princes. Therefore he offers us this formula of absolution, which, if we embraced it, would mean confessing and acknowledging that we were guilty of the crimes with which he charges us. By that very means he would not be bound by promises or by performing an oath, especially since it was decreed at the Council of Constance a hundred years ago that faith need not be kept with heretics.

units.la: Nam quod in sua Absolutionis formula subdole ac fraudulenter insinuat, peccatum, quo eos onerat, potius ex maleuolorum hominum consilio atque impulsu esse profectum, quam ex naturali ipsorum indole: nihil aliud, quam versutum quoddam commentum est, quo imprudentibus imponere, eosque sub iugum suum mittere conatur, vt ita absolutum imperium potestatemque arripiat, quoscunque ipsi visum fuerit, pro sua libidine è medio tollendi: ita vt à nemine ei exprobrari possit, quod pactis non steterit: cum semper in eius arbitrio futurum sit, quinam isti maleuoli fuerint, qui non, iudicare. Caeterum, animaduerte obsecro, clementissime Rex, quo pacto iustus Deus versipellem hunc veteratorem suo ipsius actu inuoluerit. Nam in hac ipsa absolutione, vbi nos grauissima accusatione onerare conatur, innocentiam nostram apertis verbis testatur, dicens, se nulla ratione sibi persuadere posse, nos ita a pristina integritate degenerasse, quin (nisi prauis malevolorum consiliis incitati fuissemus) in ea fidelitate animique promptitudine atque obseruantia perstitissemus, quam nos omnesque nostri maiores Maiestati tuae semper praestiterunt.
units.tr: For what he cunningly and fraudulently insinuates in his formula of absolution, namely that the sin with which he burdens them arose from the counsel and instigation of evil men rather than from their own natural disposition, is nothing but a sly contrivance. By it he tries to deceive the unwary and to bring them under his yoke, so that he may seize absolute power to remove from the midst, at his lust, whomever he pleases. Then no one could reproach him for failing to keep his pacts, since it would always rest with his judgement who those evil men were. But observe, I beg you, most clement King, how just God has entangled this shifty old trickster in his own act. For in this very absolution, where he tries to burden us with the gravest accusation, he testifies to our innocence in plain words, saying that he cannot in any way persuade himself that we had so degenerated from our former integrity, unless we had been incited by the wicked counsels of evil men. Otherwise we would have persisted in that fidelity, readiness of mind and obedience which we and all our ancestors have always shown to your Majesty.

units.la: Si enim hoc ita se habet, quod nimirum ante vltimum, vt ipse vocat, delictum omnem fidelitatem beneuolentiamque detulimus, vt ipsemet testatur, cur igitur nos multo antea omni genere crudelitatis atque inhumanitatis est insectatus? cur ciuitates ita deuastauit? oppida & vicos incendit? incolas bonis ipsorum direptis trucidauit? An non opera suorum militum Catwicum, Santfortum & Alsenum, multaque alia praeclara oppida in cineres redegit? idque multo tempore antea, vt quiritatur, quam crimen istud, quod tantopere deplorat, commissum esset? Nonne ciuitatem Vltraiectensem, quae ipsius partes prae reliquis vrbibus fouit, penitus diripere exspoliareque Albanici tentarunt? Annon Roterodami, in qua vrbe vt amici ac socii excepti fuerant, magnum ciuium numerum, contra ac promiserant, trucitarunt? An non apud Pacciecum deprehensus est catalogus innumerabilium tam nobilium, quam primae notae ciuium, qui iussu Albani diuersis in vrbibus capitali supplicio addicti erant? & in quos atrociter saeuitum fuisset, nisi summa Dei misericordia repentina mutatio rerum incidisset? At quorsum pertinebat illa decimi nummi exactio, nisi quod hoc sibi propositum habebat, vt eo pretio nostras facultates, quas omnes fisco deberi dicebat, redimeremus?
units.tr: For if this is so, and before the last offence, as he calls it, we had shown all loyalty and goodwill, as he himself testifies, why then did he long before attack us with every kind of cruelty and inhumanity? Why did he so devastate the cities? Why did he burn towns and villages, and slaughter the inhabitants after plundering their goods? Did not his soldiers, by their work, reduce Katwijk, Sandfort and Alsen, and many other famous towns, to ashes? And this, as he complains, was done long before the crime he now deplores so bitterly had been committed. Did not the Albanians attempt to completely plunder and despoil the city of Utrecht, which favoured his side above the other cities? Did they not butcher a great number of citizens at Rotterdam, where they had been received as friends and allies, contrary to what they had promised? Was not a catalogue found at Pacciecum of countless citizens, as much of the nobility as of the first rank, who by Alba's order had been condemned to capital punishment in various towns, and against whom he would have raged savagely had not a sudden change of affairs, by the great mercy of God, intervened? But to what end did that exaction of the tenth penny serve, except that he meant by that price to redeem our property, which he said was all owed to the treasury?

units.la: Ipse itaque (vt eius socii) iuratus Maiestatis tuae hostis sit necesse est, quippe qui adeo fideles Maiestatis tuae clientes, quales nos les nos fuisse ipsemet testatur, adeo immani tyrannide, cædibus, incendiis, tamque intolerabili seruitutis iugo, iam inde ab aduentus sui initio onerauit, ita vt vi quadam extremaque necessitate coacti fuerimus ad arma capessendum, eiusque atrocissimam oppressionem à nobis propulsandum: quod ne ipsi quidem eius administri inficias ire possent; cum saepenumero iactitarint, se has Prouincias earumque incolas tam diu multumque vexaturos atque irritaturos esse, donec tandē ad seditionem concitarentur, & ad rebellandum cogerentur, vt ita iustam aliquam occasionem nancisci possent, imperii in vniuersam Prouinciam inuadendi, omniaque incolarum bona pro sua libidine diripiendi. Quod quidem consilium nonnullis etiam ipsorum literis probare possemus, quibus testantur, se hanc occasionem multo antea expectasse. Verissima est, clementissime Rex, Albani hac in parte sententia: quod nimirum tui clientes nunquam à pristino statu degenerassent, nisi à maleuolis compulsi fuissent. Caeterum maleuolorum nomine non aliì censendi sunt, quam Albanus ipse cum suo senatu sanguinario, aliisque cruoris humani sitientissimis sociis, qui ex mera maleuolentia, & insatiabili auaritia iam à multo tempore clientium suorum sudorem & sanguinem suxerunt atq; exhauserunt, eosq; omni genere crudelitatis vexarunt, eoq; tandem adegerunt, vt pro sua, vxorum, liberorumq; suorū defensione, ac denique omnium eorum, quae ipsis in hac vita chara esse possunt, conseruatione, sese tueri sint coacti.
units.tr: He himself, then, as one of his associates, must necessarily be sworn an enemy of Your Majesty. He has burdened with such monstrous tyranny, slaughter and burning, and with so intolerable a yoke of servitude, from the very beginning of his arrival, clients who were, as he himself testifies, so faithful to Your Majesty, that we were compelled by a certain force and extreme necessity to take up arms and to ward off his most savage oppression. Even his own agents cannot deny this, since they have often boasted that they would harass and provoke these Provinces and their inhabitants for so long and so severely, until they were at last stirred to sedition and forced to rebel, so that they might find some just occasion for seizing power over the whole Province and plundering all the inhabitants' goods at their pleasure. We could prove this plan from some of their own letters, in which they testify that they had long awaited this opportunity. Alva's opinion in this matter is most true, most merciful King: that your clients would never have degenerated from their former state unless they had been driven to it by evil men. But by evil men none are to be understood other than Alva himself with his bloodthirsty council, and his other associates most thirsty for human blood. Out of sheer malice and insatiable greed, they have for a long time sucked and drained the sweat and blood of their clients, harassed them with every kind of cruelty, and at last forced them to defend themselves: their own persons, their wives and children, and finally the preservation of everything that can be dear to them in this life.

units.la: Quocirca quod hac in parte clementiam suam, qua in aliis ciuitatibus vsus fuit, iactitat, abunde refelli potest exèplis Tornaci, Valentianis, Insulis, Ypris, Traiecti, Dauentriae, ac deinceps Mechliniae, Aldenardi, Tenremondae, & Nardenae editis, vbi nullum direptionum, spoliorum, cædium, suspendiorum, constuprationum modum fecerunt, nullum truculentiae, immanitatisque genus praetermiserunt.
units.tr: Therefore, his boast of clemency, which he claims to have shown in other cities, can be amply refuted by the examples of Tournai, Valenciennes, Lille, Ypres, Utrecht, Deventer, and afterwards Mechlin, Aalst, Oudenaarde and Naarden, where they set no limit to plunder, robbery, slaughter, hangings and violation, and left out no kind of savagery or brutality.

units.la: Nam quod Bruxellis vltra 130. ciues ab Hispanis, diuersis temporibus, ex impotenti tantum vesania interfecti fuerint, multo ante to ante hoc inchoatū bellū: quod etiā Gandaui tumultu abHispanis excitato 60. aut 70. ciues vna atq; cadē hora, innumeri vero alii diuersis tēporib. viri pariter & mulieres ē medio sublati fuerint, hic cōmemorare nihil attinet: quum ipsi id loco summæ clementię ducant, præter id, quod in iis, quas modo diximus, ciuitatib. suma crudelitate immanitateq; perpetrarunt.
units.tr: As for the fact that more than 130 citizens of Brussels were killed by the Spaniards at various times, out of mere uncontrolled madness, long before this war began; and that at Ghent, when a riot was stirred up by the Spaniards, sixty or seventy citizens were removed from the living in one and the same hour, and countless others, men and women alike, at various times: there is no point in recounting that here, since they themselves count it as the highest clemency, apart from the cruelty and brutality with which they have committed the deeds in those cities I have just mentioned.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, non est profecto, quod nobis minetur, si modo absolutionem ab ipso oblatam non ampleætamur, nullum neque seueritatis neq; crudelitatis genus esse, qualecumque tandem illud excogitari possit, quod nobis ab illo expectandum non sit. Ita nimirum se tam in capita nostra, quam in fortunas, deuastatione, fame, gladio etiam sæuiturum, vt nullæ reliquiæ ex iis, quæ fortassis adhuc integra sunt, sint superfuturæ. Exploratissimum enim nobis est, ipsum a multo tempore nihil aliud optasse, tentasse, ac denique, quantum quidem in ipsius manu fuit, effecisse. Neque dubium est, quin longe vlterius eius crudelitas, quam tantopere iactitat, eruptura fuisset, nisi id, quod nunc euenit, timuisset: nimirum Prouincias hasce eiuscemodi immanitatem diutius non toleraturas.
units.tr: Since these things are so, there is certainly no reason for us to be threatened by him, unless we accept the absolution he offers. There is no kind of severity or cruelty, of whatever sort it may be devised, that we should not expect from him. He would rage against our heads and our fortunes with devastation, famine and even the sword, so that no remnant would survive of those things which perhaps are still intact. For it is quite clear to us that for a long time he has wished for nothing else, has attempted nothing else, and at last, so far as lay in his power, has accomplished nothing else. Nor is there any doubt that his cruelty would have broken out far beyond what he so loudly boasts, had he not feared what has now happened: namely that these Provinces would no longer endure such monstrousness.

units.la: Neque vero Regiæ Maiestatis tuæ dignitas, vel hæreditariæ Prouinciæ tuæ tantæ curæ ei sunt, vt ab iis funditus euertendis animus eius abhorreat, imo a reliquiis earum vna cum pului sculo, quod dici solet, delendis: quemadmodum frequentia incendia, vrbiumque deuastationes, quas is multo ante inchoatum hoc bellum summa crudelitate exercuit, luculentissime declarant. Cæterum bona spes nos habet, Iehouam Optim. Maximum hanc a nobis calamitate auersurum, neq; Maiestat. tuam permissurā, vt hæreditariæ ditiones tuę in eiusmodi grassatoris atq; deuastatoris manus potestatemque veniant. Nam quod hic criminatur, quod arma aduersus Maiestatem tuam sumpserimus, & tulerimus, hoc quidem negamus, & Maiestati tuæ, imo DEo, Angelisque eius testamur, nos nunquam eius animi vel consilii fuisse. Libenter enim nos nostraque Maiestatis tuæ imperio subiicimus: paratique sumus (quemadmodum in hunc vsque diem facere non desi-timus, maioresque nostri Maiestatis tuæ antecessoribus reipsa semper declararunt) ad perpetuum ac fidele Maiestati tuæ obsequium vita fortunisque nostris aduersus quoscunque tuos hostes atque aduersarios præstandum.
units.tr: Nor indeed are the dignity of Your Royal Majesty or your hereditary Provinces of such concern to him that his mind shrinks from utterly overturning them, or from destroying their remnants along with the very root, as the saying goes. Frequent fires, and the devastation of cities which he carried out with the greatest cruelty long before this war began, clearly demonstrate this. But we have good hope that Jehovah, the Best and Greatest, will turn this calamity away from us, and that Your Majesty will not permit your hereditary dominions to fall into the hands and power of such a ravager and destroyer. As for his charge that we have taken up and borne arms against Your Majesty, we deny this, and we testify to Your Majesty, yes, to God and his Angels, that this was never our intention or purpose. For we gladly submit ourselves and what is ours to the rule of Your Majesty. We are ready (as we have not ceased to do up to this day, and as our forefathers have always shown in deed to Your Majesty's predecessors) to render perpetual and faithful obedience to Your Majesty, with our lives and fortunes, against whatever enemies and adversaries you may have.

units.la: Cæterum hoc libenter vniuerso terrarum orbi testatum volumus, nos ad arma venisse, eaque fortasse (vt etiam nunc temporis facere cogimur compulsi necessitate) ad Ducis Albani, eiusque asseclarum tyrannidem immanitatemque propulsandam: vt nos, vxores, liberosque nostros, bona & vitam ab eius administrorumque suorum sanguinolentis manibus vindicare possimus, aut si illum superiorem euadere contingat, honestam potius mortem oppetamus, posterisque nostris integram laudem relinquamus, quam vt ceruices nostras sub adeo immanis tyranni iugum mittamus, charissimamque patriam nostram adeo ignominiosam seruitutem subire patiamur. Quam quidem nisi propulsaremus, non solum vbiuis locorum publicum hominum aspectum turpitudinis nostræ conscii subterfugeremus, verum etiam Maiestati tuæ, publicæque harum Prouinciarum vtilitati summum damnum inferremus. Quam certe ob causam omnes hoc inter se Ciuitates (tam communiter, quam singulæ separatim) firmiter statuerunt, vt singulæ potius (si opus fuerit) obsidionem expe-stent, & extrema omnia tentent, quin etiam omne genus miseriarum ac calamitatis ferant ac patiantur, etiam cum bonorum & vitæ amissione, imo potius flammas suis ipsorum domiciliis immittant, quam vt se in huius Tyranni imperium potestatemq; coniiciant.
units.tr: Moreover, we gladly wish this to be attested to the whole world: we have taken up arms, and perhaps (as even now we are compelled to do by necessity) we use them to ward off the tyranny and savagery of Duke Alva and his followers, so that we may rescue ourselves, our wives, our children, our goods and our lives from the bloody hands of him and his agents. Or, if it should happen that he prevails, we would rather meet an honourable death and leave untarnished praise to our descendants, than bow our necks beneath the yoke of so monstrous a tyrant and allow our dearest country to endure so shameful a servitude. Indeed, if we did not ward this off, we would not only shun the public gaze of men everywhere, conscious of our disgrace, but we would also inflict the greatest harm on Your Majesty and on the public welfare of these Provinces. For this reason all the cities have firmly resolved among themselves, both together and each separately, that each would rather await a siege (if need be) and attempt every extreme measure, and even bear and suffer every kind of misery and calamity, with the loss of goods and life; indeed they would rather set fire to their own homes than surrender themselves to the rule and power of this Tyrant.

units.la: Satis enim superque compertum habemus, ab adeo immani Tyranno, qui nobis antea ita atrociter est comminatus, & non semel fefellit, paCtaque sua iureiurando confirmata turpiter conculcauit, nullam clementiam, nullam misericordiam esse expectandam, quin potius omnes riuos ac fluuios nostro sanguine fœdaturum, omnesque arbores & patibula corporum nostrorum suspendiis oneraturum, quam vt aliquam explendæ sanguinolentæ vesaniæ suæ occasionem prætermittat.
units.tr: For we have found out well enough and more than enough that from so monstrous a tyrant, who has threatened us so savagely before and has more than once deceived us, and shamefully trampled underfoot agreements confirmed by oath, no clemency or mercy is to be expected. Rather, he would defile every stream and river with our blood, and load every tree and gallows with the hanging of our bodies, rather than let slip any occasion of satisfying his bloodthirsty madness.

units.la: Quocirca nos ad Maiestatis tuæ pedes prostrati ac supplices rogamus per nomen Dei, qui Maiestatis tuæ caput diademate, manum sceptro insigniuit, vt velis tandem causam nostram cognoscere, auresque tuas iustis & æquabilibus querimoniis nostris accommodare. Neque enim nos ab obedientia Maiestati tuæ debita subducere nitimur; sed hoc vnum petimus, vt conscientiæ nostræ Deo libere seruire posint, vtque diuinum verbum audire, & ad eius normam vitam nostram instituere, animarumque nostrarum rationem supremo omnium Iudici ad extremum illum diem reddere possimus.
units.tr: Therefore we, prostrate and suppliant at Your Majesty's feet, beg you through the name of God, who has adorned your head with the diadem and your hand with the sceptre, that you would at last deign to hear our cause, and lend your ears to our just and fair complaints. For we do not strive to withdraw from the obedience owed to Your Majesty. We ask only this one thing: that we may be able to serve God freely in our consciences, to hear the divine Word, to order our lives by its rule, and to render the account of our souls to the supreme Judge of all on that last day.

units.la: Quod vt integrum nobis sit, miseram patriam nostram, quæ ad fidelia Maiestati tuæ studia præstanda summa semper animi promptitudine parata & fuit & est, semel à grauissimo exterarum nationum & Hispanorum militum iugo liberes, iisdemque priuilegiis atque immunitatibus frui sinas, quæ Maiestas tua, & potentissimus Imperator Carolus V. Maiestatis tuæ parens, omnesque Maiores tui solemni iureiurando confirmarunt.
units.tr: So that this may be secure for us, allow our wretched country, which has always been, and still is, ready with the greatest eagerness of mind to render faithful service to Your Majesty, to be freed once and for all from the most grievous yoke of foreign nations and Spanish soldiers, and to enjoy those same privileges and immunities which Your Majesty, and the most powerful Emperor Charles V, your father, and all your ancestors confirmed under solemn oath.

units.la: Atque ita non solum arma, Maiestate tua sic iubente, deponemus, verum etiam vitam & fortunas nostras terra ac mari, quando nobis id imperaueris, libenter impendemus, speramusque, Maiestatem tuam reipsa comperturam, nos nulla ex parte deteriores degeneresque effectos esse; verum etiam maiores nostros fidelitate beneuolaq; erga Maiestatem tuam obseruantia superare. Quod quidem hac nostra testificatione Maiestati tuæ coram Deo Optimo Maxim. spondemus atque iuramus, nullam à Deo erga nos clementiam postulantes, nisi vere atque ex animo id, quod dicimus, sentiamus.
units.tr: And thus, if Your Majesty so commands, we will not only lay down our arms, but also gladly expend our lives and fortunes by land and sea, whenever you shall order us. We hope that Your Majesty will find in fact that we have become in no way worse or degenerate, but that we even surpass our forefathers in loyalty and good-willing devotion towards Your Majesty. This we pledge and swear to Your Majesty by this our declaration before God, the Best and Greatest, asking for no mercy from God towards us unless we feel truly and from the heart what we say.

units.la: Optamus etiam, vt hæc animi nostri declaratio, atque adeo iusiurandum omnibus Regibus, Principibus, Monarchis, Nationibusque innotescat, vt omnibus constet, nos nullaratione sedileditiosos, Regiq; nostro rebelles fuisse, (neque enim vllum rei exemplum à maioribus nostris accepimus) sed mera necessitate, quæ nos ad extremum premebat, coactos arma sumpsisse, iisque hostibus nomine regio abutentibus restitisse.
units.tr: We wish also that this declaration of our mind, and indeed this oath, be made known to all kings, princes, monarchs and nations, so that all may understand that we were in no way seditious or rebellious against our king (for we have received no example of such conduct from our forefathers), but that we took up arms, compelled by sheer necessity which pressed hard upon us, and resisted those enemies who abused the royal name.

units.la: Oramus itaque Christianos Principes & Monarchas, vt Christiana commiseratione nostrarum ærumnarum sese duci patiantur. Quumque facile suspicari possimus, hanc nostram petitionem, animiqué declarationem, perinde ac reliquas omnes antehac missas, suppressum iri, ita vt ad Regis nostri manus peruenire non possit, eos obnixe rogamus, vt ipsi hoc idem M. Regiæ significare, eique transmittere velint, vt causæ nostræ æquitas semel tandem in medium prodire, pleneque cognosci possit, vt Regia Maiestas se à tanta innocentis sanguinis profusione, quanta per Albanicam tyrannidem accidit, apud omnipotentem Deum purgare possit. Quod quidem omnes nos ac singuli obnixe ad Deum Optimum Maxim. pro eorum salute prosperitateque precibus, perpetuaque nostra erga eos obseruantia demereri studebimus.
units.tr: We therefore beg Christian princes and monarchs to allow themselves to be moved by Christian compassion for our hardships. And since we can easily suspect that this our petition and declaration of mind, like all the others sent before, will be suppressed so that it cannot reach the hands of our king, we earnestly ask them to be willing to signify this same thing to His Royal Majesty and to forward it to him, so that the justice of our cause may at last come into the open and be fully examined, and His Royal Majesty may be able to clear himself before almighty God of such a great shedding of innocent blood as has occurred through the tyranny of Alba. This we all and each, with our prayers to God Most Good and Greatest for their safety and prosperity, and with our constant observance toward them, will strive to deserve.

units.la: Hæitaq; Belgarum contra Ducem Alban. fuerunt querelæ. Quid vero deinceps secutum sit, id sequentium temporum annotationes indicabunt. Quid enim asperitas & tyrannis hæc Albani consequuta sit, & quantum imperium valeat, vt quod fit, hæc historia Belgica testabitur.
units.tr: Thus far were the complaints of the Netherlanders against the Duke of Alba. What followed afterwards, the records of later times will show. For what the harshness and tyranny of this Alba brought about, and how much power his rule had, this Belgian history will bear witness, as it happens.

units.la: Qui vincere aduersarium ex tuto cupit,Benignitate & gratia certet bona.
units.tr: He who desires to conquer his adversary from safety, let him contend with kindness and good grace.

units.la: DVX REQVESENIVS GVBERNATOR BELGII.
units.tr: DUKE REQUESENS, GOVERNOR OF BELGIUM.

units.la: Auraicus maximam Zelandiæ partem tenebat, Middelburgo excepto primaria Regionis vrbe, & Armuda celeberrimo illius vrbis, atque adeo totius Infulæ portu. Illam communibus nibus Insularum viribus, reliquisque suorum adiumentis obsidet.
units.tr: The Prince of Orange held most of Zealand, except Middelburg, the chief city of the province, and Armuiden, the famous harbour of that city and indeed of the whole island. He besieged it with the combined forces of the islands and the rest of his supporters.

units.la: Auxilii Middelburgensibus ferendi causa soluit Antuerpia Reg. classis ad 25. Ianuarii. In illa expeditione plura sunt passi incommoda Regii. Maius nauis ferrum exiliit, & triginta homines illo impetu, ac nonnullos e ripa prospectantes perimit. Nauis ipsa continuo vado impacta disrumpitur, alia deinde nauis, prope Omerswal, obruta vndis perit.
units.tr: To bring relief to the people of Middelburg, the royal fleet set sail from Antwerp around 25 January. On that expedition the royalists suffered several misfortunes. A cannon on one ship burst, and with that blast killed thirty men and some who were watching from the bank. The ship itself was driven onto a shoal and broke apart. Then another ship, near Omerswal, was overwhelmed by the waves and sank.

units.la: Ad Montii oppidi conspectum Reg. custodis salutandi causa, tormentariis sonitibus ludunt classiarii. In vnius nauis tormentarium puluerem ignis incogitanter iniicitur, omnesque, qui ea vehebantur, horribili spectaculo conflagrant, nec finis ille casus fuit. Instituto ad Middelburgum Regii contendunt.
units.tr: As they came in sight of the town of Montii, the sailors amused themselves with cannon salutes to greet the royal guard. In one ship, gunpowder for the cannon was carelessly set alight, and everyone aboard was burned in a horrible spectacle; nor did that disaster end there. Having set out, the royalists made for Middelburg.

units.la: Orengiani aspectante ex Bergensis oppidi ripa Requesenio, Belgii Prorege, occurrunt, acris tum pugna coorta, strenue rem vtrisque gerentibus. Ab Orengianis tamen quinque primum nauibus Regiis debellatis, & Amiraliana quidem ipsa, ab reliquis foeda fuga facta.
units.tr: As Requesens, the governor of Belgium, watched from the bank of the town of Bergen, the Orangists met the royal fleet. A fierce battle broke out, both sides fighting bravely. But first five royal ships were beaten by the Orangists, and the admiral's ship itself took to a shameful flight along with the rest.

units.la: Primus Iulianus Romanus, magni inter Hispanos nominis, fune nautico ad puppim dimissus in scapham classem deserit. Insequuntur victores Orengianici, & nouemdecim capiunt naues militares. Amiralius interficitur. Hispani omnes, atque ii quidem veterani, quotquot in potestatem venerunt, piscibus obiecti.
units.tr: First Julianus Romanus, a man of great renown among the Spaniards, was lowered by a naval rope at the stern into a skiff and deserted the fleet. The victorious Orangists pursued and captured nineteen warships. The admiral was killed. All the Spaniards who fell into their power, even the veterans, were thrown to the fish.

units.la: Middelburgicam obsidionem tum vehementer vrgere Orengianus, atqj ita paucos intra dies effectum, vt desperato auxilio, Mondragonius Middelburgensis vrbis & Armudae deditionem faceret, id fuit ad 19. Februarii iistius anni. Non repensa est expugnationis Harlemensis crudelitas lenitate, & fide vicit Auraicus maxime, sacrificulis etiam vitam condonat. Tribb. & centuriones captiuos Fliesingam mittit, data Mondragonio summo ductori illorum redimendorum facultate, qui ea de causa suae fidei interuentu, & duodecim obsidibus relictis, Antuerpiam proficiscitur, vt de captiuorum morum permutatione agat. Is Principis Auraici humanitatem, clementiam ac fidem apud Requesenium tantopere praedicavit, ut se in suspicionem apud illum & periculum aliquod conIecerit.
units.tr: Orange pressed the siege of Middelburg vigorously, and within a few days he brought Mondragón, having no hope of help, to surrender Middelburg and Armuiden. This was around 19 February of that year. The cruelty shown at the storming of Haarlem was not repaid in kind; rather, Orange conquered by good faith and, above all, by clemency, and he even granted life to the priests. He sent the captured tribunes and centurions to Flushing, giving Mondragón, their chief commander, the opportunity to ransom them. For this purpose Mondragón, on his word of honour and leaving twelve hostages behind, set off for Antwerp to arrange an exchange of prisoners. He praised the Prince of Orange's humanity, clemency and good faith so highly before Requesens that he brought suspicion upon himself and some danger with it.

units.la: Requesenius Pardonna publicat.
units.tr: Requesens publishes a pardon.

units.la: Christophorus Friderici III. Electoris filius coniunxerat se cum Ludovico Nassovio, qui ad illud usque tempus ex Montiani iurisiurandi formula ab armis abstinuerat, auxiliares 2.M. Equitum copias ad fratrem ductabat, & dum Vasconum peditatum apud Traiectum per menses duos expectat, multaque Ludovicus interim de capienda astu Antuerpiensi arce consilia init, tandem in agro Mokensi, Cliuensis ditionis, duobus Neamago milliaribus a Regiis premitur. Quumque sub vesperam acriter eorum impetum repressisset, capto Hispano quodam Lasso, magni inter eos nominis viro, postero die sub primam lucem Regiis denuo impetum facientibus, quum Ludovicus magnam equitatus partem pabulatum misisset, & peditatus Germanorum pugnam detrectaret, tandem victoria, non tamen incruenta, penes Hispanos fuit, primariis Ducibus, Christophoro & Ludovico, in eo conflictu desideratis, de quorum morte per longum tempus dubitatum est. Hoc tamen creditum est, eos tot vulneribus acceptis cecidisse, ut inter casorum cadauera diligentissime quaesiti agnosci non potuerint. Accidit ea clades 17. Aprilis istius anni.
units.tr: Christopher, son of the Elector Frederick III, had joined Louis of Nassau, who until then had abstained from arms because of the oath formula of Montigny. Christopher was leading two thousand horsemen of auxiliary forces to his brother. While he waited two months at Utrecht for the Basque infantry, Louis meanwhile made many plans to seize the citadel of Antwerp. Finally, at Mook, in the territory of Cleves, two miles from Nijmegen, he was pressed by the royalists. When at evening he had sharply repulsed their attack, he captured a certain Spaniard, Lasso, a man of great renown among them. The next day at first light the royalists renewed their attack, while Louis had sent a large part of his cavalry out to forage, and the German infantry shrank from battle. At last victory, though not bloodless, went to the Spaniards. The leading commanders, Christopher and Louis, went missing in that encounter, and for a long time their deaths were in doubt. Yet it was believed that they had fallen after receiving so many wounds that they could not be recognised among the bodies of the slain, though searched for most diligently. That disaster happened on 17 April of that year.

units.la: Requesenius de integro obsidet Leydam Duce Baldeo, quae obsidio durauit usque ad Octobrem, & tunc Hispani vi vndarum cedere coacti sunt. Sic Requesenius non magnos successus in Belgio habuit:
units.tr: Requesens again besieged Leiden under Duke Baldew, and this siege lasted until October, when the Spaniards were forced to give way to the power of the waters. Thus Requesens had no great successes in Belgium:

units.la: HISPANI LEIDAM SVBIVGARE NON QVEVNT.
units.tr: THE SPANIARDS CANNOT SUBDUE LEIDEN.

units.la: Hispani victoria Mokensi elati ad quatuor millia, quibus Auilaeus arcis Antuerpiensis Praefectus, tum exercitus Dux, 38. Mensium, qui eis debebantur, solutionem pollicitus erat, si victoria aduersus Ludovicum potirentur. Seditione facta, in vrbem Antuerpiensem (celeberrimum atque opulentissimum totius Europæ emporium) conniuentibus Hispanis, qui in arcis præsidio erant, noctu ponte per muros ducto, irrumpunt. Tunc foro occupato, stationibus que passim per vicos collocatis, pecuniam sibi persolui clamant: publicam totius vrbis direptionem minantes, nisi confestim eis satisfiat.
units.tr: The Spaniards, four thousand strong, were elated by the victory at Mook. Avila, prefect of the citadel of Antwerp and then commander of the army, had promised them payment of thirty-eight months' wages owed to them, if they gained victory over Louis. After a mutiny, they broke into the city of Antwerp, the most famous and wealthiest trading centre in all Europe. The Spaniards in the citadel garrison connived, and they came in by a bridge laid over the walls at night. Then, occupying the marketplace and posting pickets here and there through the streets, they shouted that money be paid to them, threatening the public plunder of the whole city unless they were satisfied at once.

units.la: Qua de re quum Antuerpiêses cum Prorege per literas consultant, interea per duos integros menses Hispani per vniuersam vrbem inaudita quadam insolentia grassantur.
units.tr: While the Antwerpers consulted the governor about this matter by letter, the Spaniards rampaged through the whole city for two full months with an unheard-of insolence.

units.la: Requesenius magnopere se illa Hispanorum seditione commotum simulans, (neque enim desunt, qui eum, quod ordines Belgici pecuniam antea ab eo non semel imperatam dare recusassent, omnis illius tumultus auctorem suasoremque fuisse credant) tandem numerata ab Antuerpiensibus 400. M. aureorum summa, veniam illius seditionis Hispanis dat, nullumque se vnquam eius causa communiter aut priuatim supplicium sumpturum esse, iureiurando interposito, profitetur, non sine magna omnium Ordinum indignatione. Nam ex hoc tumultu id consequutum est, vt Orengiani, vehementer clade Mockensi consternati, Hispanis tanto temporis spatio Antuerpiæ tumultuatib. animos receperint: deinde vt exterorum animis adeo atroci exemplo perterrefactis, planeque alienatis plerique se se ex ea vrbe subduxerint, omnisque negotiatio incredibilis totius Belgii iactura sit sublata.
units.tr: Requesens, pretending to be greatly disturbed by that mutiny of the Spaniards (for there are not wanting those who believe he was both the author and the instigator of the whole uproar, because the Estates of Belgium had more than once refused to give the money he had demanded), at last, after 400,000 gold pieces had been counted out by the Antwerpers, granted the Spaniards pardon for the mutiny. Under oath he professed that he would never exact punishment for it, either publicly or privately. This was not without great indignation among all the Estates. For from this uproar it followed that the Orangists, greatly dismayed by the disaster at Mook, took heart during the long time the Spaniards were rioting in Antwerp. Then, because the minds of foreigners had been so terrified by such a savage example and thoroughly alienated, most of them withdrew from that city, and all the trade of Belgium was destroyed, to incredible loss.

units.la: Accessit huc, quod, dum Hispani ipso Pentecostes die in æde S. Michaelis, quæ ad ripam Scaldis est sita, pecunia numeranda occupantur, Orengiani classem 24. nauium bellicarum omni tormentorû armorumq;, & commeatus genere instructissimam, è Scaldis alueo complurimis & ripa aspectantibus abduxerint.
units.tr: Add to this that while the Spaniards were occupied with counting out money on the very day of Pentecost in the church of St Michael, which stands on the bank of the Scheldt, the Orangists led away from the Scheldt a fleet of twenty-four warships, most fully equipped with every kind of cannon, arms and supplies, in full view of many onlookers on the bank.

units.la: Certe hoc constat, nihil vnquam ad res Principis Auraici constabiliendas, nihil ad Hispanorum vim subuertendam accommodatius, aut efficacius tumultu illo Antuerpiæ excitato accidere potuisse. Quod ipsum euentus postea docuit.
units.tr: Certainly this much is established: nothing could have been more suitable or more effective for establishing the affairs of the Prince of Orange, or for overthrowing the power of the Spaniards, than that tumult stirred up at Antwerp. The outcome itself later showed this.

units.la: M. D. LXXV.

Requesenius post iacturam Leydę & aliorum locorum in Hollandia & Brabantia, & bello diffisus de pace facienda cogitat. Postquam igitur Auraicus & Status superiore anno pacem à Rege petiuerunt: ideo locus tractationi illi eligitur Breda. Dati vtrimque obsides. Deputati à Rege voluerunt, vt omnes reciperent Papismum, qui nollent, ii certo tempore venditis bonis cederent, & vt omnia loca capta Regi restituantur.
units.tr: Requesens, after the loss of Leiden and of other places in Holland and Brabant, and distrustful of the war, began to consider making peace. Therefore, after the Prince of Orange and the States had sought peace from the King the previous year, the place Breda was chosen for those negotiations. Hostages were given on both sides. The King's deputies wanted all people to accept Papism; those who would not were to sell their goods and depart within a set time; and all places taken were to be restored to the King.

units.la: Statuum deputati libertatem conscientiarum & religionis petiuerunt, munitiones reddere detrectarunt, nihilque antequam Hispani discederent, annuerunt, sic pax non est conclusa.
units.tr: The deputies of the States asked for liberty of conscience and of religion, refused to surrender the fortresses, and agreed to nothing before the Spaniards departed; so the peace was not concluded.

units.la: Auraicus, cum multi milites ipsius iussu Antuerpiæ versarentur, ipse navibus condicto die appropinquare & urbem astu capere in animo habuit. Sed ea nocte tanta tempestas pluviarum coorta est, vt res ea à neutra parte effectui dari potuerit.
units.tr: The Prince of Orange, since many of his soldiers were in Antwerp by his order, intended himself to approach the city with ships on an agreed day and take it by stratagem. But that night such a great storm of rain arose that the plan could not be carried out by either side.

units.la: Hispani obsidet Aldenar, & præuenientes perfossionem aggerum, vi obtinent ciuitatem, & diram cladem exercent, & partem urbis comburunt. Augusto.
units.tr: The Spaniards besieged Aalst, and, anticipating the digging of the trenches, they took the town by force, inflicted a dreadful slaughter and burned part of the city. August.

units.la: Hispani obsidet Schonhofen, quam egregie tuebatur Monsieur Garde. Sed cum muri dempti essent, certis conditionibus eam tradit.
units.tr: The Spaniards besieged Schoonhoven, which Monsieur de Gaarde defended splendidly. But when the walls had been taken down, he surrendered it on certain conditions.

units.la: Requesenius omne studium confert, ad occupandam Regionem Zerizeæ, vt postea Walkerum, & hoc modo totam Hollandiam & Zelandiam subiugare posset. Ita cum Armada Tholum venit, & ad flumen fortalitia excitat, mense Septembri.
units.tr: Requesens devoted all his effort to occupying the region of Zierikzee, so that afterwards he could subdue Walcheren and in this way the whole of Holland and Zeeland. Thus with the fleet he came to Tholen and built forts along the river, in September.

units.la: Venit cum navibus D. Auila Capitaneus Hispanus, versus Zirizeam, & Bomenedem. Ciuitatulam obsidet & vi capit, & omnes trucidat, post Zirizeam obsidet, & flumen cathenis coniungit, vt naues Auraicas cohibeat.
units.tr: Don Avila, a Spanish captain, came with ships towards Zierikzee and Bommenede. He besieged the small town, took it by force, and put everyone to the sword; afterwards he besieged Zierikzee, and joined the river with chains, so as to restrain the Orange ships.

units.la: M. D. LXXVI. Auraicus in Februario obtinet fortalitium Crimpen ad fluuium Lik. Ita vicina loca inter Dotrecht & Roterodamum defensa manebant.
units.tr: 1576. In February the Prince of Orange won the fort of Krimpen on the river Lek. So the neighbouring places between Dordrecht and Rotterdam remained defended.

units.la: Dum haec geruntur, Requesenius peste obit Bruxellis 15. Martii.
units.tr: While these things were happening, Requesens died of plague at Brussels on 15 March.

units.la: Requesenius in sua gubernatione occupauit Alcmar, Dordmund & Zirizeam, & fudit Ludouicum Nassoui- um, & Christophorum Palatinum. Sed amisit Mittel- burg, & Leidam frustra obsedit, & ab eius morte magnæ confusiones sequutæsunt. Nam Hispani rebellarunt, & Status vniti sunt.
units.tr: In his government Requesens occupied Alkmaar, Dordrecht and Zierikzee, and routed Louis of Nassau and Christopher the Palatine. But he lost Middelburg, and besieged Leiden in vain; and after his death great confusions followed. For the Spaniards rebelled, and the States united.

units.la: REGIVM CONSILIVM RES BEL- GICAS ADMINI- STRAT.
units.tr: THE KING'S COUNCIL ADMINISTERS THE AFFAIRS OF THE NETHERLANDS.

units.la: Tunc Consiliarii generales Statuum, seu Ordines gene- rales, gubernacula sumunt, & Petrum Ernestum Mansfel- dium gubernatorem Luzemburgensem in ducem belli assu- munt. Et institutum hoc Regi probatur, in quo aliquid momenti fore sperauit. Et Auraicus quidem amissis tot vr- bibus, & Zirizea obsessa in angustiis versabatur. Et classis, quam in auxilium Zirizeæ misit, dissipata, & Zirizea capta est.
units.tr: Then the general counsellors of the States, or the General Estates, take up the reins of government and appoint Peter Ernest Mansfeld, governor of Luxembourg, as commander of the war. The King approved this arrangement, hoping it would bring some advantage. William of Orange, indeed, having lost so many towns, was in difficulties, and Zierikzee was under siege. The fleet he sent to relieve Zierikzee was scattered, and Zierikzee was taken.

units.la: Nota. Vt nuper post occupatam Harlem, & cladem in Mekenhard aduersitates Regiorum secutæ sunt: sic nunc post captam Zirizeam, & alios prosperos successus, sequuntur graues motus.
units.tr: Note: just as after the capture of Haarlem and the defeat at Mekeren the royalists suffered reverses, so now, after the capture of Zierikzee and other successes, grave disturbances follow.

units.la: Nam Hispani, cum magnas difficultates in sterilibus Insu- lis passi essent, rebellant, & in Brabantiam concedunt. Bru- xellenses igitur metuentes rebellium vim arma contra Hi- spanos capiunt. Manlsfeldius quidem cum Hispanis agit, ve- rum illi in defectu pecuniæ non sedantur, & Alostum concedentes eam spoliant & vastant, Iulio.
units.tr: For the Spaniards, after suffering great hardships on the barren islands, mutinied and moved into Brabant. The people of Brussels, therefore, fearing the power of the rebels, took up arms against the Spaniards. Mansfeld indeed negotiated with the Spaniards, but since they lacked money they were not pacified; withdrawing from Alost, they plundered and devastated it, in July.

units.la: Consilium Statuum Brabantiæ Hispanos etiam pro prodi- toribus publico scripto propter multas causas proclamat. Vnde irritati Hispani, minus quam antea placari se patiuntur.
units.tr: The council of the States of Brabant also proclaimed the Spaniards traitors by public writ, for many reasons. Provoked by this, the Spaniards allowed themselves to be appeased even less than before.

units.la: Consilium Brabantinum cum videret, Consiliarios Statuum cum rebellibus colludere & consentire, Senatum illum Regium Bruxellis captiuauit, nempe Mansfeldium, Barlemontium, Assouilleum, & duos Secretarios, & sic statim Dux de Arschot Princeps Ciuitatis Bruxellensis nominatur, & isti alias etiam Ciuitates in suas partes adducere moliti sunt, quo communi opera exteros ex patria propellere possent.
units.tr: When the Brabant council saw that the councillors of the States were colluding and agreeing with the rebels, they seized that royal council at Brussels, namely Mansfeld, Barlemont, Assonleville and two secretaries. At once the Duke of Aarschot was named Prince of the city of Brussels, and these men also tried to bring other cities over to their side, so that by common effort they could drive the foreigners out of the country.

units.la: Quidam ex Consilio Statuum Brabantiæ suaserunt, vt Alanzonius Regis Galliæ frater adscisceretur in protectorem Brabantiæ, ad quam rem illi operam suam prompte contulit. Huic fœderi se coniunxerunt, de consilio Rennebergeri, Status Hannoniæ, cum Flandri, Resselt, Donai, Artois, & aliæ Prouinciæ.
units.tr: Some of the council of the States of Brabant advised that Alençon, brother of the King of France, be taken on as protector of Brabant, and he promptly gave his effort to this cause. On the advice of Rennenberg, the States of Hainault joined this league together with Flanders, Resselt, Douai, Artois and other provinces.

units.la: Consiliarii stantes à parte Regis cum rebellibus agunt, sed nihil obtinent.
units.tr: The councillors who stood on the King's side negotiated with the rebels, but achieved nothing.

units.la: Regii igitur, quos habebant milites, hinc inde collegerunt, & confugium suum in Castellum Antuerpiense habuerunt, sub Duce Sancho de Auila. Prospexit sibi etiam Capitaneus in Lier Romero, & Capitaneus in Maestrich Montesdoque.
units.tr: The royal soldiers they had were gathered from here and there, and they made their refuge in the citadel of Antwerp under Duke Sancho d'Avila. The captain at Lier, Romero, also provided for his own safety, and the captain at Maastricht, Montesdoca.

units.la: Status contra militem collegerunt, operam dantes, ne Hispani simul coniungi possent.
units.tr: The States gathered troops against the soldiers, taking care that the Spaniards could not be joined together.

units.la: Status cum Hispanis ad Louanium dimicantes, & qui seipsis studiosi miscuerunt, fusi sunt ab Alenzo de Vergas. Deinde Status ad Walhen circiter 800. ceduntur.
units.tr: The States, fighting with the Spaniards near Louvain, and those who eagerly threw themselves into the fray, were routed by Alonso de Vargas. Then the States near Walhain were cut down, about 800 of them.

units.la: Alenzo de Vergas Maestricum occupat, ne Status militem isthic traducere possent.
units.tr: Alonso de Vargas occupied Maastricht, so that the States could not move troops across there.

units.la: Confoederati instituunt occupare Antuerpiam Ciuitatem, vt sic & Castellum obtinere possent. Euocant igitur praesidiarios suos ex Bruxella, Mechlinia, & Louanio, Duce Philippo Egmondano. Iuncti sunt & alii proceres, sic, vt extiterint circiter 6. M. militum. Hi die 3. Nouembris venerunt ante Antuerpiam.
units.tr: The confederates resolved to seize the city of Antwerp, so that they could also obtain the citadel. They therefore summoned their garrisons from Brussels, Mechelen and Louvain, under Duke Philip of Egmont. Other nobles joined them, so that there were about 6,000 soldiers. These came before Antwerp on 3 November.

units.la: Perenot & Eberstein Præsides vrbis fidem dederant, quod vrbem pro Rege seruare vellent vsque ad aduentum Iohannis Austriaci. Horum, fidei immemorum, consensu copiæ confœderatorum vrbem cum gaudio sunt ingressi. Et dum nebulæ essent, ita vt Hispani tormentis damnum iis inferre nequirent, sese communiuerunt. Et quamuis deinde ex arce seu castello maximis fulminibus tonaretur: tamen ab opere sese muniendi non destiterunt, quin & fœminæ visæ sunt absque terrore aliquid operæ conferre. Præsides arcis erant Rodes & Auila.
units.tr: Perrenot and Eberstein, the governors of the city, had given their pledge that they would keep the city for the King until the arrival of John of Austria. Forgetful of this pledge, by agreement the forces of the confederates entered the city with joy. And while there were mists, so that the Spaniards could not harm them with artillery, they fortified themselves. And although afterwards a great thunder of bolts came from the citadel or castle, yet they did not desist from fortifying themselves; indeed women were seen contributing to the work without fear. The commanders of the citadel were Rhodes and Avila.

units.la: Capitaneus Ortys ex castello vrbem inuasit, & magnam stragem in vrbe inter milites edidit.
units.tr: Captain Ortiz attacked the city from the castle and made great slaughter among the soldiers in the city.

units.la: Rebelles Hispani, qui in Alosto fuerunt, audientes sonitus bombardarum, opinantes id quod erat, ex Castello in vrbem Antuerpiam ita tonari, vltro adcurrunt.
units.tr: The rebel Spaniards who were in Aalst, hearing the sound of the cannon and supposing what was in fact the case, that the city of Antwerp was being bombarded from the castle, hurried there of their own accord.

units.la: Conueniunt & ex aliis & satis longe dissitis locis & præsidiis Hispani, & per posticum in Castellum intromissi statim, etiam cibo contempto, cum magno impetu ex Castello egressi, & precibus ad Mariam & S. Iacobum factis, munitiones superant, vrbem inuadunt, omnia sternunt, Curiam duabus tonnis Ducatorum ædificatam, cum hominibus igni exurunt, combustæ etiam 600. ædes. Elapsi sunt Dominus Haure, & alii, qui in Zelandiam ad Auraicum peruenerunt. Obersteinius cum naue nimium hominibus repleta aquis perierunt, & sic opulentissima & splendidissima vrbs & maximæ opes miserrima clade exiguo momento excisæ sunt quinto Nouembris, Anno
units.tr: Spaniards also gathered from other and rather distant places and garrisons. Once admitted through the postern into the castle, even without taking food, they went out from the castle with great impetus; after prayers offered to Mary and St James, they overcame the defences, invaded the city, overthrew everything, and burned the Court, built at a cost of two tuns of ducats, along with its people; 600 houses were also burned. Lord Haure and others escaped and reached Zeeland, to William. Obersteyn perished with a ship too crowded with men, in the waters.
